name: trilogy-styles-tokens
description: "Design Trilogy component styles with semantic variables, modes, and React Native styles during Figma and code synchronization."
---

# Trilogy Component Styles and Tokens

1. Inspect the component's Web styles, semantic tokens, theme, and Native context. Map UI props, component classes, values, and Figma variables, including Light/Dark modes. Do not confuse semantic variables with primitives, and do not assume identically named values match across platforms.
2. Distinguish component variants from explicit overrides by analyzing their actual role in the design, code, and request—not by name alone. The following are **non-exhaustive examples**, not a closed list or automatic classification: a prop such as `variant` or `status`, or `size` when it selects a complete Figma variant, may choose a component class whose SCSS contains all styles for that variant. A prop that directly specifies a visual property, such as `color`, `background`, or `fontWeight`, may be an optional helper override even if Figma exposes it as a variant. Apply the same reasoning to other relevant props, inspect available helpers and conventions, and ask if the role remains ambiguous. For `Title` and `Text`, `size` selects the complete variant: do not create a separate `fontSize` prop unless explicitly requested; `fontWeight` allows a weight override. Do not automatically create redundant overrides for other components. Do not impose an incompatible rename without approval.
   - When no helper prop is provided, add no helper class or synthetic override value: the component variant determines its default rendering. When a helper prop is provided, add the corresponding existing helper class alongside the variant class; it must override only that property without replacing other variant styles. Verify actual cascade and specificity, not merely class presence. Do not duplicate helper rules in component SCSS or create a missing helper without a decision.
   - Treat the shared `CommonProps.style` as an explicit consumer customization escape hatch, similar to `className`, not as a named design variant. On Web, forward `CSSProperties` to the rendered element; on Native, accept React Native `StyleProp<ViewStyle | TextStyle>`. Apply it after built-in styles so caller values take precedence. It is a code-only property and does not require a Figma variant or mapping.
   - On React Native, reproduce the same precedence with themed styles: base and variant styles first, then only explicitly provided overrides. Preserve existing behavior and visual parity without HTML classes.
   - Explicitly connect classes emitted by the Web render to selectors actually defined in component SCSS: base class, variants, states, and defaults. Verify the SCSS file is included in the styles package exports and every conditional class has a matching rule; do not merely declare styles without applying them.
   - For an HTML element rendered directly by a created or modified component, assemble its classes with `clsx` and apply `useHashClass(clsx(...))`, including base, variant, and supplied `className` according to existing conventions. Call the hook unconditionally at the component's top level before any return.
   - When rendering a Trilogy component inside another component, pass un-hashed classes (optionally assembled with `clsx`) if the child accepts `className` and applies `useHashClass` itself. The child hashes these classes once; do not hash them in the parent. Verify the actual child implementation: do not assume a third-party or polymorphic component hashes classes, and do not omit required hashing on HTML elements rendered directly by the parent.
3. Helpers in `packages/styles/src/helpers/` are for explicit visual overrides and remain available to consumers. Default variant styles belong to the component; overrides must use existing helpers. Preserve custom classes and other components. Do not change shared helpers without need and without considering compatibility.
4. On Native, use the existing context, `makeStyle`, semantic tokens, and custom modes/themes. Place each component's styles in its own colocated `<name>.styles.native.ts`; each styled subcomponent owns and imports its own style file, never the parent's file. Do not create empty style files. Verify platform differences in cascade, fonts, and behavior. Do not change functional logic to fix appearance.
5. For Figma, follow the `design-figma` skill: bind visual properties to appropriate semantic variables, never directly to primitives. Preserve aliases, values, and modes; do not change shared tokens for one component without authorization. Never create a variable collection, mode, or variable (the file only has Primitives, Dimensions, Colors, and Fonts): express token choices as variant or instance properties bound to existing semantic variables, as the `design-figma` skill defines. Do not reproduce unverified values or behavior. Report hardcoded values, missing tokens, or differences between code and Figma.
